schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch lay out the chapter's structure (altar and feast, vv.1-7; foundation, vv.8-13) and date the assembly to the year of return; Ellicott marks Tisri as the most solemn month and 'as one man' as one consent, not all.
Henry reads a portrait of zeal: a newly-returned people, still homeless among ruins, leaving their business to gather 'as one man' at God's altar, worldly business postponed to religion.
Clarke pictures the exiles lodging in huts among the ruins before rearing the altar and keeping the feast; Wesley notes the sacred, festival-filled month.
Gill fixes Tisri as the month 'approaching,' the altar reared before it had fully come.

Keil reads the two leaders with priests and laity restoring the legal sacrifices, the altar finished by the first of the month; Ellicott: the altar is 'only the beginning,' the temple to be built around it as the centre.

Clarke traces Jeshua's descent from the martyred high priest Seraiah, making him the first high priest after the captivity; Wesley gives three reasons the altar preceded the temple — atonement, assistance, and strengthening of hearts and hands.
Gill names Jeshua the high priest, the proper person to lead the work.
Henry draws the lessons: begin with God, and do what we can in worship when we cannot do what we would — no temple yet, but not without an altar.

Keil and Ellicott read 'upon his bases' as the altar's old site found among the ruins — the new only a restoration of the old — and the fear as dread of the surrounding heathen, driving them to secure divine protection near the altar.
Clarke: though fear was upon them, yet they built the altar; Wesley: because of fear they made the more haste, for apprehension of danger should quicken us to duty and drive us to God.
Gill: the altar was fixed on the same spot where it had stood before, on what remained of the old.

themes: the altar on its old site
fear of the people of the land

schools.summary: Keil unfolds the descending daily offerings of the feast (Num. 29:13ff.), counted beast by beast; Ellicott presses the intent — a stress on the entire renewal of the Mosaic economy of service.

Clarke fixes the feast's dates (fifteenth day, offerings from the first); Wesley takes 'tabernacles' as standing for all the month's solemnities, since they would not have neglected the Day of Atonement.
Gill: kept 'as it is written,' beginning the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
Henry: the feast was seasonable — recalling the fathers' tents and pointing, per Zech. 14, to gospel times.

Keil defines the order — the daily offering first, then new moons and annual feasts and the freewill nedabah offered from free inclination; Ellicott takes the verse as general and anticipatory, the whole ritual fixed before the temple was built.
Gill guards the order: the daily sacrifice was never begun only after the feast but always taken first, the special sacrifices after.
Wesley marvels at the freewill offerings: the law required much, but they, poor in wealth and rich in zeal, offered more.
Henry: they spared at their own tables to supply God's altar plentifully — a holy heat brought out of the furnace of affliction.

Ellicott and Keil read the verse as recapitulation and hinge: sacrifice restored from the first of the month, but the temple foundation not yet laid — a clause pointing forward to the building that fills the rest of the chapter.
Gill marks the first day as new moon and feast of trumpets, and doubts not they kept the tenth-day Atonement.
Wesley: 'burnt offerings' is often put in Scripture for all the sacrifices offered on the feast of trumpets.

Keil details the corn, wine, and oil paid to Sidon and Tyre for Lebanon cedar floated to Joppa, all after Solomon's precedent; Ellicott marks the distinction — Jews paid in money, Phoenicians in kind (cf. Acts 12:20) — and the port and Cyrus's grant.
Clarke sees a deliberate copying of Solomon's conduct (1 Kings 5:11), the same Tyrian craftsmen hired by Cyrus's leave and supplied in kind.
Gill: money given the masons and carpenters to buy stone and timber for the temple.
Henry: what God calls us to, we may depend on his providence to furnish; Tyre, Sidon, and Lebanon supplied as of old.

themes: cedar to the sea of Joppa

schools.summary: Keil marks the formal commencement — Levites from twenty years up appointed to oversee the work; Ellicott dates it to Zif, B.C. 537, the very month of Solomon's first foundation, the Levites' age matching David's ordinance (1 Chron. 23).
Henry weighs the prompt, hearty resolve — 'well begun is half ended' — and the one heart God gave magistrates, ministers, and people for the work.
Gill reconstructs the winter gap: the exiles settled their cities, then returned in spring to build, the materials readied and rubbish cleared.
Clarke: the prior time was spent clearing ground, felling timber, hewing and transporting stones.

Keil and Ellicott sort the three Levite orders, read 'sons of Judah' as a slip for 'sons of Hodaviah' (Ezra 2:40), and confess the sons of Henadad's absence from that list an insoluble puzzle; the fewness of overseers made good by their unanimity and vigour.
Gill cautions that this Jeshua is the Levite (Ezra 2:40), not the high priest.
Wesley agrees — a Levite, not the high priest — and reads their task as urging the workmen to a vigorous prosecution.

themes: not the high priest but the Levite

schools.summary: Keil sets priests in their robes with trumpets and Asaphite Levites with cymbals; Ellicott makes the principle explicit — as the offerings followed Moses, so the music followed David, trumpets to priests and cymbals to Levites by ancient ordinance.
Clarke: praise with the psalms David composed, done in the very manner he directed.
Gill: the builders who laid the foundation were the masons, whose proper work it was.
Henry: a concert of trumpet and cymbal, not to please the ear but to assist the everlasting hymn.

themes: priests with trumpets, Levites with cymbals

schools.summary: Ellicott: they answered antiphonally, in chorus, the shout a religious acclamation; Keil records the old view (via Exod. 15:21) of two choirs, one singing 'the LORD is good,' the other 'his mercy endureth for ever.'
Henry presses the clause 'toward Israel' — mercy enduring toward a people once captive and estranged; the church continues because that mercy continues (Ps. 73:1).
Gill: they sang by course, in responses, one company answering another.
Wesley: the everlasting hymn, the burden of Psalm 136 — God is good, and his mercy fails not.

Wesley and Clarke catalogue the losses that drew the old men's tears — the ark, the Urim and Thummim, the shechinah, the fire, poorer and narrower foundations — and point to Haggai's comfort that the latter house's glory would exceed the former.
Henry balances the two sounds: some reason for the tears if they mourned the sin behind the change, yet an infirmity to damp the common joy and despise the day of small things.
Ellicott: the weeping sprang not from any mere comparison of size but from the thought of the great desolation, the younger looking to the future; the scene needs Haggai 2 and Zechariah 4.
Gill: the weeping ancients were men of seventy or eighty who had seen the first house.

debates.question: Was the old men's weeping wholly warranted?

sides.position: a just grief over a departed glory and the real losses of the second house (ark, Urim, shechinah, poorer foundations)
in part an infirmity that damped the common joy and despised the day of small things

themes: the departed glory of the first house

schools.summary: Keil clarifies that both joy and weeping arose among all the people and could not be told apart because the shout was so loud; Ellicott vouches 'all here has the stamp of truth' in the blended, far-heard cry.
Henry reads the blended noise as an image of this world — joy and grief never yet cleanly parted — bidding us rejoice with the joyful and weep with the weeping.
Gill: the two sounds were so mixed and confounded that they made a jarring discord.
